summary: Defines the Certification Authority Authorization DNS record, which lets a domain holder list the certification authorities allowed to issue certificates for that name. Public CAs can check it to reduce the risk of mis-issued certificates. The document specifies the record syntax and the rules for processing it. It obsoletes RFC 6844.

plainLanguage.summary: A CAA record lets the owner of a domain name list the certificate authorities that are allowed to issue certificates for it. A certificate authority checks that record before issuing anything, so a mistake at an authority that is not on the list cannot produce a certificate for that name.

questions: how to restrict certificate issuance for a domain
subtitle: A DNS record that tells certificate authorities which of them may issue certificates for a domain.

tldr.problem: Any of the hundreds of public certificate authorities can issue a certificate for any domain name, which means a mistake or a compromise at one of them can produce a certificate for someone else's site.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a CAA resource record. A domain holder publishes it in the DNS to name the certificate authorities allowed to issue for that name, and a compliant authority must check the record before it issues anything.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8659 replaces RFC 6844 with a simpler rule for finding the record that applies, a clearer grammar for the issue and issuewild tags, and a new section on the errors CAs hit when looking up CAA records in practice.

facts.label: Reserved flag bits
facts.value: Must be cleared to 0 and ignored

today: RFC 8659 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 6844 and is the current definition of the CAA resource record, including the rule a certificate authority follows to find the record that applies to a name.

sections.title: What a CAA Record Does
sections.content:
The Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS Resource Record lets a DNS domain name holder specify the Certification Authorities (CAs) authorized to issue certificates for that domain name. Publishing CAA Resource Records allows a public CA to implement additional controls to reduce the risk of unintended certificate mis-issue.

Like the TLSA record defined in DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE), CAA records are used as part of a mechanism for checking PKIX certificate data. The difference is one of timing: CAA records specify an authorization control to be performed by a CA before issuing a certificate, and TLSA records specify a verification control to be performed by a Relying Party after the certificate is issued.

Conformance with a published CAA record is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the issuance of a certificate. A set of CAA records describes only current grants of authority, and because certificates are valid for a period of time, a certificate that does not match the records published now may have matched the records published when it was issued. Relying Parties MUST NOT use CAA records as part of certificate validation, though Certificate Evaluators MAY use them as a possible indicator of a security policy violation.
sections.plainLanguage: Any public certificate authority can issue a certificate for any name, so a slip or a compromise at one of them can hand out a certificate for somebody else's website. A CAA record lets the domain owner say which authorities are allowed to act for that name.

sections.title: Finding the Relevant Record Set
sections.content:
Before issuing a certificate, a compliant CA MUST check for publication of a Relevant RRset. If such an RRset exists, the CA MUST NOT issue a certificate unless it determines that the certificate request is consistent with the applicable CAA RRset, or that an exception in the relevant Certificate Policy or Certification Practices Statement applies. If the Relevant RRset contains no property tags that restrict issuance, for instance if it contains only iodef tags or only tags the CA does not recognize, CAA does not restrict issuance.

The search climbs the DNS name tree from the specified label up to, but not including, the DNS root, until a CAA RRset is found. Given a request for an FQDN X or a wildcard domain name *.X, the Relevant RRset is determined by querying for CAA at X, removing the leftmost label to get the parent, and repeating while the domain is not the root. The pseudocode in the RFC works through this with the name X.Y.Z, where no CAA records exist at any level, and then with A.B.C where a record named issue example.com sits at B.C and the climb stops there.

A certificate request MAY specify more than one FQDN and MAY specify wildcard domain names. Issuers MUST verify authorization for all of the FQDNs and wildcard domain names in the request.
sections.plainLanguage: The authority looks for a CAA record at the exact name first. If there is none, it drops the leftmost part of the name and looks again, and keeps going up towards the root until it finds one record set. That record set is the only one that matters for that name.

sections.title: The Syntax of a CAA Record
sections.content:
A CAA resource record contains a single property consisting of a tag-value pair. An FQDN MAY have multiple CAA records associated with it, and a given property tag MAY be specified more than once across them. The RDATA section holds one property made of a flags field of one octet, a tag length field of one octet, the tag itself, and the value. Where n is the length given in the tag length field and m is the number of remaining octets in the value field, they are related by m = d - n - 2, where d is the length of the RDATA section.

Bit 0 of the flags field is the Issuer Critical Flag. If it is set, the property is critical, and a CA MUST NOT issue certificates for any FQDN if the Relevant RRset contains a critical property with an unknown or unsupported tag. Following the DNS conventions, bit 0 is the most significant bit, so the flags value 1 means that bit 7 is set while a value of 128 means that bit 0 is set. All other bit positions are reserved, MUST be cleared to zero, and MUST be ignored on receipt.

The tag length MUST be at least 1. Tags may contain the ASCII letters and the digits 0 through 9 and nothing else, and matching of tags is case insensitive. The canonical presentation format of the record is CAA, the flags as an unsigned integer between 0 and 255, the tag in lowercase, and the value as either a contiguous set of characters without interior spaces or a quoted string.
sections.plainLanguage: Each CAA record carries one tag and one value, with a flags byte in front. The critical flag says that a certificate authority must understand this tag before it issues anything for the name, and the tag length byte says how long the tag is.

sections.title: The issue, issuewild and iodef Properties
sections.content:
If the issue tag is present in the Relevant RRset for an FQDN, it asks issuers to perform CAA issue restriction processing and to grant authorization to issue certificates containing that FQDN to the holder of the issuer-domain-name, or to a party acting under that holder's explicit authority. The value follows a sub-syntax written in ABNF, in which the issuer domain name is given first and any parameters follow after a semicolon. FQDN values are specified in letter-digit-hyphen label form.

An issue tag with no issuer-domain-name requests that no certificates be issued, so a record reading CAA 0 issue ";" forbids issuance by any issuer. A malformed issue value that does not match the grammar is treated the same way, as an empty issuer-domain-name. Authorizations are additive, so listing an empty issuer-domain-name alongside a non-empty one has the same effect as listing only the non-empty one. An issuer MAY add parameters that constrain issuance further, and the semantics of those parameters are determined by the issuer alone.

The issuewild tag has the same syntax and semantics as issue except that it grants authorization only for certificates that specify a wildcard domain name, and each issuewild property takes precedence over each issue property when specified. An issuewild property MUST be ignored when the request is not for a wildcard domain name, and if at least one issuewild property is present for a wildcard request, each issue property MUST be ignored for that request.

The iodef property gives a way to report certificate issue requests that violate the security policy of the issuer or of the name holder. It takes a URL, and the scheme decides how the report is sent: mailto sends an email with the Incident Object Description Exchange Format report as a MIME attachment, and http or https submits the report as a web service request. Those are the only supported schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: The issue tag names the authorities allowed to issue for the name, and an empty one forbids issuance by everyone. The issuewild tag does the same job but only for wildcard names such as *.example.com, and it wins over issue when both are present. The iodef tag gives an address at which to report attempted issuance that breaks policy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CAA records assert a security policy that the holder of an FQDN wishes issuers to observe, so their effectiveness as an access control mechanism depends on issuers obeying them. The objective of the record is to reduce the risk of certificate mis-issue rather than to avoid reliance on a certificate that has been mis-issued.

The use of DNSSEC to authenticate CAA records is strongly RECOMMENDED but not required. An issuer MUST NOT issue certificates if doing so would conflict with the Relevant RRset, irrespective of whether the DNS records are signed. DNSSEC verification lets an issuer tell an empty answer apart from a suppressed one, and lets it archive proof that it was authorized to issue for the name.

The use of CAA records does not prevent mis-issue by an authorized CA, so FQDN holders SHOULD verify that the CAs they authorize employ appropriate controls. Suppression of a CAA record or insertion of a bogus one could let an attacker obtain a certificate from an issuer that was not authorized. Where DNSSEC is not deployed, an issuer SHOULD use other DNS security controls, and data cached by third parties MUST NOT be relied on as the sole source of CAA information.
sections.plainLanguage: CAA only works if the certificate authorities actually obey the records. It also only protects against authorities that are not on the list; an allowed authority that mis-issues is still a problem. Signing the records with DNSSEC is strongly recommended, so that a forged or hidden record can be detected.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
A CA implementing CAA may find that it receives errors when looking up CAA records. Some middleboxes, in particular anti-DDoS appliances, may be configured to drop DNS packets of unknown types, or may start dropping them when they consider themselves under attack. This generally appears as a timed-out query or as a SERVFAIL at a local recursive resolver. Some authoritative nameservers respond with REJECTED or NOTIMP when queried for a record type they do not recognize, and at least one authoritative resolver produces a malformed response, with the query/response bit set to zero, when queried for unknown types. The correct response code for unknown record types is 0, no error condition.

Some FQDN administrators make the contents of a subdomain unresolvable on the public Internet by delegating it to a nameserver with a private IP address. A CA processing CAA records for such subdomains receives SERVFAIL from its recursive resolver and MAY interpret that as preventing issuance. Administrators wishing to issue certificates for private FQDNs SHOULD use split-horizon DNS with a publicly available nameserver, so that CAs receive a valid, empty CAA response.

Queries for CAA records differ from most other record types, because a signed empty response is meaningfully different from a bogus response. A signed empty response means there is definitely no CAA policy at that label, while a bogus response may mean a misconfigured zone or an attacker tampering with records. Implementations may have bugs with signatures on empty responses that go unnoticed, because for common types such as A and AAAA the difference between empty and bogus does not matter to an end user.
sections.plainLanguage: In practice, looking up CAA records fails in recognisable ways. Firewalls that drop unusual DNS packets, name servers that answer unknown types with an error, and subdomains that are delegated to private name servers all produce failures. The document lists them so that authorities can tell their subscribers what to fix.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 6844
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 6844. The most important change is to the processing section, which is now called Relevant Resource Record Set. RFC 6844 specified an algorithm that performed tree climbing not only on the FQDN being processed but also on all CNAMEs and DNAMEs encountered along the way. That made processing inefficient for names that use many CNAMEs, and would have made it hard for hosting providers to set CAA policies on their own names without also setting unwanted policies on their customers' names. This document specifies a simplified algorithm that only climbs the tree for the FQDN being processed and leaves the handling of CNAMEs and DNAMEs to the CA's recursive resolver.

The document also clarifies the ABNF grammar for the issue and issuewild tags and resolves inconsistencies with the earlier text, in particular by specifying that parameters are separated with semicolons. It also allows hyphens in property tags, and it clarifies the processing of a CAA RRset that is not empty but contains no issue or issuewild tags. The section on the CAA RR type was merged into the mechanism section, and the section on the use of DNS security was moved into the security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version of this record made authorities climb the DNS tree for every alias they met along the way, which was slow and hard for hosting companies to use. This version climbs only for the name being asked about and leaves the rest to the resolver.
